lectures.title: Digital Assets, Tokenization, and NFTs - lesson slides
Digital Assets, Tokenization, and NFTs - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A startup says it has tokenized concert tickets because it minted one token for each seat. What is the most important follow-up question from the lesson's framing of tokenization?
questions.correct_answer: What rights or claims does each token reference, and who or what enforces admission, transfer rules, and refunds?
incorrect_answers: Which consensus mechanism does the underlying ledger run, and what is the exact average block time of the validator network?
What metadata standard is used to host the ticket artwork, and how many graphic designers were hired for the launch?
Which resale marketplace has leading volume, and how much seed capital did the ticket startup disclose publicly at launch?
questions.explanation: The lesson frames tokenization as programmable representation of rights, claims, or references, not merely putting labels on-chain. The key analysis is what the token means and which on-chain or off-chain systems enforce that meaning.

questions.question_stem: Which classification best matches the lesson's taxonomy of digital assets and trust models?
questions.correct_answer: Native coins support chain operation, fungible tokens track interchangeable balances, NFTs track unique identifiers, and asset-backed tokens depend on external custody or legal arrangements.
incorrect_answers: Native coins govern legal claims, fungible tokens represent unique physical items, NFTs track purely interchangeable balances, and asset-backed tokens exist entirely without external custody or audits.
Native coins represent media files, fungible tokens dictate validation protocols, NFTs track underlying cash reserves, and asset-backed tokens operate without any off-chain legal arrangements.
Native coins verify ownership rights, fungible tokens track non-fungible art, NFTs govern consensus-level block rewards, and asset-backed tokens require absolutely no third-party enforcement at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates technical form from trust model. Different asset categories imply different accounting assumptions and different external dependencies.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Asset Taxonomy And Trust Models / Essential Concepts

questions.question_stem: A game wants one token type for identical gold coins and another for individually named swords with different attributes. Which design implication best follows from fungibility?
questions.correct_answer: Gold coins should use balance-style accounting, while swords need unique identifiers, metadata, and ownership records for individual items.
incorrect_answers: Gold coins must use unique cryptographic identifiers, while swords require simple balance-style tracking to ensure high transaction throughput.
Gold coins should require individual metadata files, while swords need off-chain consensus-based validation rules to verify game attributes.
Gold coins must require external legal custodians, while swords need proof-of-stake validation mechanisms to enforce standard transfer rules.
questions.explanation: Fungible assets emphasize interchangeable quantities, balances, allowances, and arithmetic. Non-fungible assets emphasize token IDs, metadata integrity, provenance, and rights clarity.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Fungibility As A Design Constraint / Fungible vs Non-Fungible -- Design Implications

questions.question_stem: A buyer claims, "I bought the NFT, so I automatically own the copyright and can force every marketplace to remove copies." What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: The NFT usually gives control of the token; copyright, commercial rights, takedowns, and platform access require separate legal terms or platform policies.
incorrect_answers: The NFT automatically transfers exclusive copyright; licensing, commercial usage, duplication, and hosting require zero legal terms or contract policies.
The NFT permanently prevents digital duplication; reproduction, online distribution, screenshotting, and viewing require mandatory smart contract rules.
The NFT technically secures absolute legal title; physical ownership, trademark rights, commercial profits, and royalties require no off-chain rules.
questions.explanation: The lesson repeatedly separates token ownership from media ownership, copyright, platform rights, and legal enforcement. Clear licenses can reduce ambiguity, but token control alone does not create every off-chain right.
questions.lesson_block: NFTs: What Are We Actually Buying?
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: NFTs As Layered Systems, Not Just Tokens / Common Misconceptions And Confusions

questions.question_stem: An NFT project stores metadata at ordinary HTTPS URLs controlled by the project team. What risk should an auditor highlight?
questions.correct_answer: The metadata is cheap and flexible, but the operator can change or remove what the URL serves unless other controls exist.
incorrect_answers: The metadata is fully consensus-secured, but validators can edit or delete what the host serves unless users pay extra gas.
The metadata is immutable, but client apps can replace token identifiers whenever block times increase sharply.
The metadata is trustless by design, but the contract can rewrite chain history if creators sign a special update.
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts on-chain storage, content-addressed storage, and location-addressed URLs. HTTPS links are convenient but mutable and operator-dependent, so token ownership can remain correct while displayed content changes or disappears.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Storage, Metadata, And Integrity / Metadata and Storage Models

questions.question_stem: A collection uses content-addressed storage for its NFT media. Which statement best captures the improvement and the remaining dependency?
questions.correct_answer: The content hash makes tampering detectable, but someone still must preserve, pin, or pay for the content to remain available.
incorrect_answers: The content hash guarantees copyright protection, but the project team still must host, monitor, or manage the legal licensing agreements.
The content hash prevents third-party duplication, but the client wallet still must decode, execute, or render the raw binary files.
The content hash automates royalties, but marketplaces must record secondary sales before the contract pays creators.
questions.explanation: Content-addressed storage ties references to content hashes, so changed content no longer matches the reference. That integrity benefit does not itself guarantee long-term availability.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Storage, Metadata, And Integrity / Common Misconceptions And Confusions

questions.question_stem: A marketplace report shows a collection has many transfers, a long ownership history, and a few high-price sales. What is the safest conclusion under the lesson's provenance discussion?
questions.correct_answer: Provenance can document origin and transfers, but it does not by itself prove value, healthy demand, or absence of wash trading.
incorrect_answers: Provenance can guarantee commercial copyrights, but it does not by itself prove validity, metadata persistence, or system decentralization.
Provenance can secure asset redemption, but it does not by itself prove safety, operator integrity, or absence of price inflation.
Provenance can prevent resale copying, but it does not by itself prove scarcity, code quality, or absence of trading bots.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes verifiable history from market quality. Provenance can support authenticity and scarcity claims, but thin liquidity, hype, or wash trading can distort price signals.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Tokenization Promises And Their Limits / Provenance / Market Design, Royalties, And Fairness

questions.question_stem: A creator points to an on-chain royalty preference and says it guarantees payment on every secondary sale. Which explanation best matches the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Royalty standards can communicate preferred payments, but marketplaces and transfer pathways decide whether and how to honor them.
incorrect_answers: Royalty standards can automatically seize buyer funds, but validators and consensus protocols decide whether and how to process them.
Royalty standards can permanently lock transfer pathways, but creators and smart contract developers decide whether and how to release them.
Royalty standards can guarantee copyright claims, but courts and IP offices decide whether marketplaces must honor them.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats royalties as marketplace-dependent signals rather than universal resale guarantees. A standard may publish a preference, but enforcement depends on ecosystem behavior and market incentives.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Market Design, Royalties, And Fairness / Royalties as marketplace-dependent signals

questions.question_stem: A generative NFT mint reveals rare traits before allocation is finalized. Which design change best reduces selective-minting risk?
questions.correct_answer: Use a commit-reveal or verifiable-randomness approach so minters cannot reliably target known rare traits before allocation is finalized.
incorrect_answers: Publish all rare metadata schemas immediately so users cannot easily predict individual trait combinations before the mint is finalized.
Use location-addressed hosting URLs so administrators cannot modify image attributes before the mint allocation is finalized.
Enforce strict creator royalty signatures so external marketplaces cannot list individual items before allocation finalizes.
questions.explanation: The lesson connects trait visibility to selective minting. Commit-reveal schemes and VRF-style randomness can reduce predictable allocation games, though they do not solve every launch problem.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_05-EF-digital_assets_tokenization_and_nfts-slides-only.qmd: Market Design, Royalties, And Fairness / Minting and Market Design Patterns

questions.question_stem: A token claims to represent one ounce of gold held by a custodian. Which audit focus best reflects the lesson's RWA analysis?
questions.correct_answer: Verify custody, audits, redemption rules, legal agreements, jurisdiction, and data integrity in addition to the token contract.
incorrect_answers: Inspect consensus, blocks, validator sets, gas limits, node counts, and transaction throughput in addition to the token contract.
Analyze metadata, artwork, image resolution, content hashes, file formats, and storage directories in addition to the token contract.
Evaluate ticker names, decimals, UI fields, transfer methods, and standard events as complete proof of the gold reserves.
questions.explanation: Real-world asset tokens inherit off-chain dependencies. The token may automate transfers or claims, but credibility rests on custodians, legal structures, audits, redemption processes, and jurisdictional enforcement.

questions.question_stem: According to the ERC-20 reading, why does a common token interface matter for wallets and decentralized exchanges?
questions.correct_answer: They can interact with many fungible token contracts through shared methods and events instead of building a custom integration for each token.
incorrect_answers: They can guarantee identical economic value across diverse token issuers through automated on-chain pricing instead of building custom software updates.
They can execute instant zero-gas token conversions through direct peer-to-peer consensus channels instead of deploying smart contract methods on Ethereum.
They can bypass ledger validation rules through isolated state channels instead of verifying token balances for every transfer attempt.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes ERC-20's ecosystem value as a standardized API for fungible tokens. Shared functions and events make tokens legible to wallets, exchanges, and applications, but do not standardize value or implementation details.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/erc20_ethereum_org.txt; /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/eip20.txt: Standardization And Interoperability / Core Reading Takeaways

questions.question_stem: A user calls `approve` for a decentralized exchange contract and sets a large ERC-20 allowance. What has happened according to the reading?
questions.correct_answer: The user has authorized that spender to move up to the approved amount later, typically through `transferFrom`; `allowance` reports the remaining authorized amount.
incorrect_answers: The user has transferred that specific balance to the spender immediately, typically through `approve`; `totalSupply` reports the remaining authorized amount.
The user has burned that approved asset amount permanently, typically through calling `transferFrom`; `balanceOf` reports the remaining authorized amount.
The user has locked that maximum supply limit indefinitely, typically through standard `allowance`; `transfer` reports the remaining authorized amount on-chain later.
questions.explanation: The reading distinguishes `approve`, `allowance`, and `transferFrom`. Delegated spending lets another address initiate transfers up to an approved amount instead of moving tokens immediately at approval time.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/eip20.txt: Delegated Spending / approve, allowance, and transferFrom

questions.question_stem: Two ERC-20 tokens both expose the expected interface and emit standard events. What conclusion is best supported by the reading?
questions.correct_answer: Software can observe and call them in standard ways, but interface compliance does not make implementation quality, gas behavior, or optional metadata choices identical.
incorrect_answers: Software can convert and trade them in trustless ways, but interface compliance does make their underlying security, economic value, or issuer backing identical.
Software can ignore and bypass them in automated ways, but interface compliance does force their operational execution, gas limits, or private functions identical.
Software can compile and deploy them in consensus ways, but interface compliance does guarantee their optional symbols, decimal scales, or name lengths identical.
questions.explanation: The reading treats ERC-20 compliance as interface standardization. Required methods and events support interoperability, while optional `name`, `symbol`, and `decimals` fields and implementation choices remain project-specific tradeoffs.
